17.attempt: choose the most common cause and declare certainty
17.failure: this works until the rare tiger arrives. Refusing to decide is safer intellectually but useless when the camp must act
17.repair: keep every plausible outcome and give each a share of belief. Count comparable past observations, then divide the count for one outcome by the total

18.attempt: ask which story is generally more believable
18.failure: that ignores the actual print. Or ask for the probability of the story directly, although the story is what we are trying to judge
18.repair: reverse the question: if this story were true, how expected would the observed evidence be?

19.failure: a long predictable greeting can contain less news than one unexpected word. Use raw surprise such as one divided by probability, but independent surprises then multiply instead of add
19.repair: we need rare events to carry more information, certain events to carry none, and independent messages to add. The negative logarithm satisfies all three needs

20.failure: both bags contain stones, and both have two named colors if we list an absent possibility. Or inspect only the most likely outcome, losing the rest of the distribution
20.repair: average the information of every possible outcome, weighted by how often that outcome occurs

21.attempt: use zero for correct and one for wrong
21.failure: it treats barely wrong and confidently wrong as equal. Use ordinary distance between probabilities; it does not directly price the information wasted by the prediction
21.repair: charge the information cost assigned by the predicted distribution to the outcome that actually occurred

22.attempt: try a large jump and keep it if loss falls
22.failure: large jumps can leap over improvements. Try every possible value; there are infinitely many
22.repair: nudge the weight by a tiny amount, observe the change in loss, and divide change in loss by change in weight. Then imagine the nudge shrinking toward zero

23.attempt: measure only the first effect or only the final effect
23.failure: either breaks the causal path. Recompute the whole network separately for every weight; that repeats enormous amounts of work
23.repair: we need to multiply local sensitivities along the causal path. Each stage tells how strongly it passes a small change onward

24.attempt: perturb each weight and rerun the model
24.failure: this needs at least one extra forward pass per weight. Or trace paths independently and calculate the same suffix again and again
24.repair: compute the prediction once, remember intermediate values, then move backward. At each node, reuse the blame already accumulated from everything downstream

25.attempt: jump directly opposite the gradient with no step control; the model may overshoot and diverge
25.failure: take microscopic steps; learning may take forever. Trust one example; its noisy advice can undo another
25.repair: move every parameter a controlled distance opposite its gradient, repeat on batches of examples, and watch loss rather than assuming progress

26.failure: it is fast, but noisy accidents dominate. Use every observation before each update. It is stable, but painfully slow and cannot react until the whole archive is read
26.repair: average the evidence from a small group. Each batch is large enough to soften accidents and small enough to update frequently

27.attempt: always take a huge step: leap across the valley and oscillate
27.failure: always take a microscopic step: improve so slowly that the expedition ends first
27.repair: multiply the gradient by an adjustable positive step size, observe whether loss descends, and adjust that size over time

28.failure: sideways noise repeatedly cancels progress. Average every past gradient equally; ancient advice remains influential after the landscape changes
28.repair: keep a fading memory of past gradients and combine it with the new one

29.failure: neurons receive identical evidence and remain identical. Use arbitrarily huge random values. Signals explode or gates saturate
29.repair: draw small random weights whose scale depends on how many inputs feed the neuron

30.failure: depth increases, but expressive power does not. Use a hard yes-or-no threshold; it creates decisions but supplies almost no useful gradient
30.repair: place an activation after a linear transformation. ReLU opens positive paths; smoother gates such as GELU vary them gradually

31.failure: the model may have memorized scratches and shadows. Make the model infinitely flexible; it can store even more irrelevant detail
31.repair: we need to reserve unseen cases and compare training success with performance outside the training memory

32.attempt: forbid complexity by making the model too small; it may lose real structure too
32.failure: stop training at an arbitrary time without observing unseen performance
32.repair: add a cost for large weights, remove random paths during training, or stop when validation performance stops improving

33.attempt: use training loss for every choice; it rewards memorization
33.failure: check the test set repeatedly; every decision leaks test information back into development
33.repair: split data by role: training changes weights, validation changes design decisions, and test data is opened once at the end

34.attempt: assume all future observations come from exactly the same source as training
34.failure: or demand good performance on every imaginable world, which no finite evidence can guarantee
34.repair: state the deployment world, test meaningful shifts, and build representations around relationships likely to survive those shifts

35.attempt: hide everything behind a framework call
35.failure: the code runs, but the causal chain disappears. Hand-tune outputs without gradients; every new example breaks the tuning
35.repair: we need to build a two-layer network, cache its intermediate values, backpropagate every derivative, update on batches, and evaluate on unseen data

36.attempt: give every complete word one ID
36.failure: spaces appear to provide the boundaries
36.repair: use characters. Any new spelling can now be represented

37.attempt: feed token IDs directly into the network
37.failure: since 417 is larger than 92, arithmetic treats tiger as greater than lion. The distance from tiger to lion becomes 325, while the distance from tiger to token 418 is one
37.repair: give every vocabulary item a one-hot vector: one coordinate is one and all others are zero. `lion → [1, 0, 0, 0]`, `tiger → [0, 1, 0, 0]`, and `river → [0, 0, 1, 0]`. Now IDs no longer pretend to contain magnitude

38.attempt: sort tokens by ID or trust their array slot without exposing it to the model
38.failure: the first invents arbitrary order; the second stores position outside the computation
38.repair: add a position-specific vector to each token vector before attention. Content says what; position says where

39.attempt: train each prefix in a separate forward pass
39.failure: it prevents cheating but repeats nearly identical work
39.repair: we need to process all positions together while blocking attention from position i to every later position j

40.attempt: treat an entire sentence as one training example with one answer
40.failure: most of its transitions provide no learning signal
40.repair: shift the sequence by one position so every visible prefix predicts the token immediately following it

41.attempt: choose the nearest input embedding directly
41.failure: that restricts the scoring rule and hides how every vocabulary candidate should compete
41.repair: use a learned linear map to produce one raw score for every vocabulary item

42.attempt: divide each logit by their sum
42.failure: negative values break probability and shifting all scores changes the result
42.repair: exponentiate relative scores, normalize them, then charge the negative log probability of the observed next token

43.failure: the same prompt follows the same narrow path. Sample raw probabilities blindly. Low-quality tail tokens eventually derail the text
43.repair: we need to control the distribution with temperature and optionally restrict it to a credible top set before sampling

44.attempt: attend to the entire history forever
44.failure: computation and memory grow, and the model eventually exceeds positions it was trained to handle
44.repair: choose a maximum context, train within it, and reuse cached keys and values during generation instead of recomputing the unchanged past

45.attempt: call a framework Transformer and hide the causal chain
45.failure: or connect the parts without checking shapes, leakage, and target alignment
45.repair: assemble token and position embeddings, masked Transformer blocks, vocabulary logits, cross-entropy training, and iterative sampling in one traceable program

46.attempt: count how many generated sentences sound good. The sample is small, decoding choices interfere, and two people may disagree
46.failure: the held-out sentence “the tiger sleeps” reveals the weakness. Model A assigns the observed tokens probabilities 0.5, 0.5, and 0.5; Model B assigns 0.9, 0.1, and 0.9. A few attractive samples cannot expose B’s severe surprise at the middle token
46.repair: score the probability assigned to every actual next token, combine those costs, and convert the average back into an intuitive “equally likely choices” scale

47.attempt: choose one benchmark score and call it intelligence
47.failure: the trouble appears immediately: a calculator can ace arithmetic while failing conversation; a fluent model can pass style tests while inventing facts. One number silently chooses which failures do not matter
47.repair: we need to name the intended job, create separate tests for its required abilities and risks, and inspect real failures rather than averaging them away

48.attempt: trust fluent language because uncertainty should sound hesitant
48.failure: training rewards plausible continuations. A fabricated citation can match the shape of real citations and therefore sound more natural than “I do not know.”
48.repair: separate linguistic plausibility from supported knowledge. Require evidence, permit abstention, and test whether claims can be traced to an available source

49.attempt: treat the largest softmax probability as honest confidence
49.failure: collect ten answers each reported near 80%. If only four are correct, the number is not describing observed reliability
49.repair: group predictions with similar confidence and compare their average stated confidence with the fraction actually correct

50.attempt: collect as much text as possible and assume scale washes out bad examples
50.failure: duplicated false claims become louder, rare high-quality explanations become quieter, and sensitive records remain memorized. More observations amplify whatever process produced them
50.repair: treat data construction as part of the model: trace provenance, remove harmful duplication, filter carefully, preserve valuable diversity, and document choices

51.attempt: make the model as large as possible and assume capability follows parameter count
51.failure: a huge model trained on too little data repeatedly studies the same evidence; abundant data cannot help a model too small to compress its patterns
51.repair: we need to run controlled experiments across sizes, fit the observed trend, and balance model capacity, data, and compute rather than worship one number

52.attempt: prompt more forcefully and hope next-token prediction infers the desired interaction
52.failure: the trouble appears immediately: given “Translate cat to French,” raw continuation may produce more translation examples, commentary, or unrelated web text. Pretraining learned many formats, not one cooperative policy
52.repair: show many instruction-input-response examples and continue training so following the requested task becomes a reusable pattern

53.attempt: write one perfect target response for every prompt and train only to imitate it
53.failure: many answers can be valid. A single target penalizes harmless alternatives and cannot express that answer A is preferred to B without being the only possible answer
53.repair: collect comparisons between candidate responses, learn which properties predict preference, and use that signal to improve the response policy

54.attempt: retrain the whole model whenever one document changes
54.failure: a price changes today, a policy changes tomorrow, and private documents cannot all be baked into public weights. Retraining is slow and still hides the source
54.repair: search an external collection for evidence relevant to the question, place that evidence in context, and generate an answer grounded in what was retrieved

55.attempt: ask the language model to simulate every tool from memory
55.failure: it invents live weather, makes arithmetic errors, and cannot know whether an external action succeeded
55.repair: we need to let the model choose a permitted tool, provide structured arguments, observe the real result, and decide the next step under explicit limits

56.attempt: give every available tool to the model and treat user intent as unlimited permission
56.failure: ask for an itinerary and watch the agent buy a nonrefundable ticket. The plan was requested; the purchase was not
56.repair: separate capability from authority. Give the smallest permissions needed, attach scope and limits, and require confirmation before consequential actions

57.attempt: place tool results directly into the prompt and let the model obey whichever instruction sounds strongest
57.failure: the trouble appears immediately: a restaurant review can now command the booking agent. Untrusted content crosses from data into control
57.repair: label provenance, keep instructions separate from evidence, restrict tools independently of model text, and reject actions whose authority comes only from retrieved content

58.attempt: ask the agent to take the next action that sounds useful until the goal appears complete
58.failure: it changes DNS before verifying the new server, loses the rollback path, and discovers a missing database only after users arrive
58.repair: represent the goal as ordered steps with prerequisites, expected evidence, risk, and rollback conditions. Re-plan when observations contradict assumptions

59.attempt: store every message forever and paste all history into every new prompt
59.failure: cost grows, irrelevant details drown current evidence, contradictions accumulate, and sensitive information persists without purpose
59.repair: we need to separate short-term working context from durable memory. Store only useful facts with source, time, scope, and a way to update or forget them

60.attempt: let the conversation prose serve as the workflow state
60.failure: the model says “refund completed” after merely drafting it, or issues it twice after losing track of an earlier tool result
60.repair: represent allowed states and transitions explicitly. Move state only when required evidence arrives from the responsible system

61.attempt: trust the absence of an error message or the model’s own description of its work
61.failure: the changed code compiles but breaks another case. Confidence is not evidence of the requested outcome
61.repair: define success before acting, then collect independent evidence: tests, queries, rendered output, checksums, or user-visible state

62.attempt: retry the action whenever a response is missing
62.failure: the trouble appears immediately: the first payment succeeded and the retry charges the customer twice
62.repair: give each logical action a stable idempotency key, query existing state, and make repeated requests return the first result instead of repeating the effect

63.attempt: create many agents for every problem and let them freely edit shared state
63.failure: they duplicate searches, contradict one another, overwrite files, and consume more time coordinating than solving
63.repair: we need to delegate only separable work with explicit ownership, inputs, outputs, and merge rules. Keep one accountable coordinator for the final result

64.attempt: log only the final response, or log every hidden detail without structure
64.failure: the first gives no diagnosis; the second creates an unreadable, expensive, privacy-sensitive transcript
64.repair: record structured events for decisions, tool calls, state changes, costs, timing, evidence, and outcomes while redacting sensitive content

65.attempt: give the agent a broad goal and let it continue until it believes the goal is complete
65.failure: a mistaken assumption triggers a long plan, repeated actions increase damage, and no one notices until after an irreversible step
65.repair: create an explicit operating envelope: allowed goal, tools, budgets, states, approval gates, verification requirements, stop conditions, and escalation path

66.attempt: treat every click as independent evidence of natural preference
66.failure: show one song repeatedly; its extra clicks now appear to prove it deserved repetition
66.repair: record how the system influenced each observation and evaluate outcomes against a control or exploration policy

67.attempt: retrain immediately on every new labeled event
67.failure: the trouble appears immediately: one mislabeled transaction can move the model before anyone notices
67.repair: we need to update from controlled batches with validation, rollback, and limits on how quickly behavior may change

68.attempt: assume training accuracy remains valid forever
68.failure: a winter-trained demand model meets summer behavior and keeps reporting confident old patterns
68.repair: monitor input, prediction, and outcome distributions; investigate meaningful shifts before retraining

69.attempt: compare this week with last week
69.failure: a holiday raises sales for both systems and receives credit as a model improvement
69.repair: randomly assign comparable cases to old and new behavior and compare predefined outcomes

70.attempt: always choose the currently best option
70.failure: an unlucky first result permanently hides a better alternative
70.repair: reserve some choices for exploration while exploiting accumulated evidence

71.attempt: search for one neuron dedicated to each human concept
71.failure: the concept disappears when one neuron is removed yet can still be decoded from a pattern across many neurons
71.repair: we need to treat representations as distributed directions and test them across varied examples

72.attempt: train a powerful classifier on hidden states and call any success evidence
72.failure: the trouble appears immediately: the probe learns the task itself even if the representation did not make it simple
72.repair: use a deliberately limited probe and compare layers, controls, and baselines

73.attempt: remove each word and treat output change as complete explanation
73.failure: removing a word changes grammar and creates an unnatural new input
73.repair: measure sensitivity with several methods and test whether highlighted evidence changes behavior under controlled interventions

74.failure: limited width forces useful patterns to share neurons, producing confusing mixed activations
74.repair: represent features as directions that can overlap when they rarely need to be active together

75.attempt: assume correlation with output proves causation
75.failure: the direction predicts answers but changing it leaves behavior unchanged
75.repair: we need to intervene on the representation and measure the specific downstream change against controls

76.attempt: assign one label to the entire raw byte sequence
76.failure: a one-pixel shift changes thousands of byte positions although the same tiger remains
76.repair: preserve local spatial arrangement and compare nearby color measurements

77.attempt: learn a separate edge detector for every location
77.failure: the trouble appears immediately: the model relearns the same pattern thousands of times and fails when it moves
77.repair: slide one small learned filter across all positions and reuse its weights

78.attempt: keep every activation at full resolution through every layer
78.failure: memory explodes and tiny shifts move evidence to neighboring cells
78.repair: summarize small neighborhoods while retaining the strongest or average evidence

79.attempt: classify directly from isolated edge responses
79.failure: one edge has no object-level meaning
79.repair: we need to stack local detectors so later layers combine earlier patterns over wider regions

80.attempt: treat every pixel as a token
80.failure: the sequence becomes enormous and individual pixels carry little stable structure
80.repair: group pixels into patches, embed them as tokens, add position, and apply attention

81.attempt: copy the input through an unrestricted hidden layer
81.failure: a wide hidden layer learns identity without compression
81.repair: force information through a bottleneck and train reconstruction

82.attempt: assume any compressed coordinates form a smooth useful space
82.failure: the trouble appears immediately: tiny code changes can cause abrupt unrelated outputs
82.repair: shape the latent distribution and train nearby codes to decode coherently

83.failure: independent pixels produce noise because neighboring colors and shapes constrain one another
83.repair: we need to choose an order and predict each piece from previously generated pieces

84.attempt: map one random vector directly to a finished image in one jump
84.failure: one enormous jump is difficult to learn and unstable across diverse images
84.repair: gradually add noise to real images, then learn the smaller reverse step at every noise level

85.attempt: ask it to recreate the entire clean image directly from every noise level
85.failure: the task changes dramatically across noise strengths
85.repair: tell the model the noise level and predict the added noise or equivalent clean direction

86.attempt: label the correct action at every moment
86.failure: for exploration or games, nobody knows every correct intermediate move
86.repair: provide outcome feedback and let experience connect actions with later consequences

87.attempt: store only action and final reward
87.failure: the trouble appears immediately: the same action helps in one situation and harms in another
87.repair: we need to record current state, chosen action, reward, and resulting state

88.attempt: choose the action with the largest reward right now
88.failure: a small immediate treat can prevent reaching a larger later reward
88.repair: estimate the future reward expected from a state or state-action pair

89.attempt: replace its value with the immediate reward
89.failure: the update ignores the valuable state reached afterward
89.repair: move the estimate toward reward plus the best discounted value available next

90.attempt: always choose the highest estimated action
90.failure: early errors remove exploration and discrete choice blocks ordinary differentiation
90.repair: sample from a policy and increase probability of actions followed by better-than-expected returns

91.attempt: compare raw pixels directly with token IDs
91.failure: their coordinates have unrelated meanings and shapes
91.repair: we need to use separate encoders and train paired image-text examples to become nearby

92.attempt: pull every observed pair together without negatives
92.failure: the trouble appears immediately: all representations can collapse to one point
92.repair: compare each true pair against mismatched alternatives in the same batch

93.attempt: treat every raw sample as an independent token
93.failure: sequences are huge and local frequency structure is hidden
93.repair: transform short windows into time-frequency features, then model their sequence

94.attempt: copy and fine-tune all parameters for every task
94.failure: storage and training cost multiply, and the base model is harder to preserve
94.repair: freeze the base and learn a small low-rank correction to selected matrices

95.attempt: round every weight aggressively without measuring effect
95.failure: small but important distinctions disappear and outputs degrade
95.repair: we need to map values to a limited set of levels using calibrated scale and test sensitive layers

96.attempt: let many machines train independent copies and combine them occasionally
96.failure: their parameters drift and duplicated work wastes computation
96.repair: partition data or model work, synchronize required results, and preserve one coherent update

97.attempt: run one request at a time on one full model
97.failure: the trouble appears immediately: hardware sits idle between small operations and traffic spikes create queues
97.repair: batch compatible requests, cache repeated state, schedule fairly, and enforce resource limits

98.failure: real users, attackers, and accidents find paths designers never listed
98.repair: actively search for failures, record reproducible cases, and turn discoveries into regression tests and mitigations

99.attempt: let builders decide every acceptable use because they understand the system
99.failure: affected users carry risks without authority, appeal, or visibility
99.repair: we need to define ownership, review, documentation, incident response, user recourse, and deployment boundaries

100.attempt: connect every powerful component and call the result intelligent
100.failure: an accurate model with stale data, excessive authority, weak verification, or no accountability still fails
100.repair: build one observable loop where evidence, representation, prediction, action, verification, feedback, and governance constrain one another

101.attempt: represent every uncertainty with one low confidence number
101.failure: a clearer image can repair blur, but not missing knowledge; more training data can repair missing knowledge, but not a genuinely coin-flip outcome
101.repair: separate uncertainty in the observation from uncertainty in the model’s knowledge

102.attempt: discard the old belief and use only the newest clue
102.failure: the trouble appears immediately: one noisy footprint can overpower years of evidence
102.repair: combine prior plausibility with how expected the clue is under each story, then normalize across stories

103.attempt: trust one training run as the unique learned truth
103.failure: different initialization and data order produce different boundaries
103.repair: we need to train several diverse models and combine predictions while inspecting disagreement

104.failure: thousands of easy repeated cases consume effort while the decision boundary remains unclear
104.repair: ask for labels where the model is uncertain or where examples add new coverage

105.failure: a forced answer converts uncertainty into confident-looking error
105.repair: allow abstention and choose a coverage level whose retained answers meet a risk target

106.attempt: fine-tune only on the newest data
106.failure: updates useful for B overwrite weights carrying A
106.repair: rehearse old evidence, protect important parameters, or allocate new capacity

107.attempt: periodically retrain from scratch on everything
107.failure: the trouble appears immediately: storage and compute grow forever, and old raw data may be unavailable
107.repair: we need to detect change, consolidate stable knowledge, adapt limited components, and evaluate past and present tasks together

108.failure: a new task with different labels requires many examples and broad retraining
108.repair: optimize prior parameters or an update rule so a few new examples produce useful adaptation

109.attempt: shuffle all examples uniformly from the beginning
109.failure: early gradients from unsolved complex cases are noisy and provide little structure
109.repair: order or weight examples so mastered foundations support harder cases, while revisiting earlier skills

110.attempt: wait for humans to label every example
110.failure: labels are expensive and discard most structure already inside observations
110.repair: hide or transform part of an observation and train the model to recover the missing relation

111.attempt: learn only which action was rewarded in previously visited situations
111.failure: the agent cannot imagine untried sequences or reuse physical regularities
111.repair: we need to learn a compact model that predicts next state and reward from current state and action

112.attempt: treat every correlation as a controllable cause
112.failure: the trouble appears immediately: hot weather raises both; changing one does not necessarily change the other
112.repair: represent plausible causal structure and distinguish observing a variable from intervening on it

113.attempt: compare them with any untreated person
113.failure: differences in age and illness confound the comparison
113.repair: construct a comparable alternative world using causal assumptions and matched evidence

114.attempt: commit to the first sequence imagined
114.failure: one forecast may exploit model error or miss better branches
114.repair: simulate multiple candidate sequences, score outcomes, act briefly, observe reality, and plan again

115.failure: most computation is wasted on obviously poor branches
115.repair: we need to balance exploring uncertain branches with deepening promising ones, then propagate outcomes backward

116.failure: a lucky answer hides invalid reasoning; one arithmetic slip ruins an otherwise sound plan
116.repair: represent intermediate claims and verify each with an appropriate checker or evidence source

117.attempt: force fuzzy perception into rigid rules or exact rules into learned approximation
117.failure: the trouble appears immediately: the first breaks on noisy inputs; the second can violate guaranteed constraints
117.repair: let neural components propose symbols or scores and symbolic components enforce explicit relations

118.attempt: store every fact as an isolated sentence
118.failure: repeated entities, reverse links, and multi-hop questions become difficult to traverse
118.repair: represent entities as nodes and named relations as edges

119.attempt: assign a fixed input slot to every possible neighbor
119.failure: graphs vary in size and neighbor order should not change meaning
119.repair: we need to apply the same message rule to each edge and aggregate neighbor messages without depending on order

120.failure: a new input exposes the absence of an underlying algorithm
120.repair: search or generate candidate programs, execute them, and keep those satisfying examples and constraints

121.attempt: add more random tests and call the property proven
121.failure: an untested edge case can remain
121.repair: state assumptions and desired properties formally, then prove or mechanically check that every transition preserves them

122.attempt: remove names and assume records are anonymous
122.failure: the trouble appears immediately: rare combinations and model outputs can re-identify individuals
122.repair: limit how much any one record can change the released result, usually by clipping influence and adding calibrated noise

123.attempt: upload every user record to one server
123.failure: central collection increases privacy and governance risk
123.repair: we need to send model updates to devices, train locally, aggregate protected updates, and return a shared model

124.failure: an attacker follows the model’s sensitivity into a brittle direction
124.repair: search for worst-case permitted perturbations, train against them, and bound behavior where possible

125.attempt: let it generate experiments, change itself, and deploy improvements automatically
125.failure: a flawed metric or experiment compounds through self-modification before external review
125.repair: separate hypothesis generation, sandboxed experiment, independent evaluation, authority, reproducibility, and approved deployment

126.attempt: ask whether more context makes the model better
126.failure: better at what, on which examples, compared with what baseline? Any result can be declared a success after the fact
126.repair: state one predicted change, one intervention, one measurement, and one observation that would count against the claim

127.attempt: ship both improvements and compare with the old system
127.failure: the trouble appears immediately: one score changed while two possible causes changed; the result cannot assign credit
127.repair: we need to hold everything fixed except the suspected cause, and include a control that receives no intervention

128.attempt: keep the best checkpoint and report its score
128.failure: changing only the random seed makes the gain disappear
128.repair: record code, data, configuration, environment, seeds, and variation across repeated runs

129.attempt: let each model demonstrate its strongest example
129.failure: a showcase cannot support comparison because difficulty and scoring move with the contestant
129.repair: freeze representative tasks, inputs, metrics, and scoring rules before seeing results

130.attempt: assume held-out files guarantee unseen knowledge
130.failure: the same questions appeared online in training data with small formatting changes
130.repair: track provenance, search for semantic overlap, use time-separated tests, and create private fresh evaluations

131.attempt: generate millions of answers and train on all of them
131.failure: confident errors are copied, multiplied, and eventually treated as truth
131.repair: we need to generate candidates, verify what can be verified, preserve diversity, mix trusted data, and track ancestry

132.attempt: train a small model only on the original hard labels
132.failure: the trouble appears immediately: the labels reveal the winner but discard how the teacher distributed doubt among alternatives
132.repair: let the student imitate the teacher's probability pattern as well as the observed answer

133.attempt: run every specialist for every token and average them
133.failure: most computation is wasted on specialists irrelevant to the current token
133.repair: learn a router that sends each token to a small number of experts while balancing their workload

134.attempt: keep full attention and buy more hardware
134.failure: doubling length roughly quadruples pairwise comparisons
134.repair: preserve a small pattern of local, global, or retrieved connections that matches the task's information paths

135.attempt: append every past event to every future prompt
135.failure: cost grows forever and important facts drown in irrelevant history
135.repair: we need to write selected facts to addressed storage, retrieve by present need, and preserve provenance and update rules

136.attempt: assume information inside the window will automatically influence the answer
136.failure: availability is not retrieval; distracting passages dominate the relevant line
136.repair: test whether the clue can be located, ranked, and used, then combine retrieval with focused reasoning

137.attempt: make every model response extremely long
137.failure: the trouble appears immediately: easy tasks waste computation while long fluent mistakes become more convincing
137.repair: allocate extra attempts or steps only when uncertainty and verification justify their cost

138.attempt: ask the same generator to confidently approve its own first answer
138.failure: the error that shaped the proposal also shapes its self-justification
138.repair: generate diverse candidates, check them with independent evidence, and keep only paths that survive

139.attempt: reward only whether the final answer matches
139.failure: lucky shortcuts receive the same credit as reliable reasoning
139.repair: we need to evaluate checkable intermediate claims and train the system to prefer valid paths

140.attempt: increase the reward whenever the dirt sensor reads zero
140.failure: the agent covers the sensor instead of cleaning the room
140.repair: treat reward as imperfect evidence, monitor side effects, use multiple checks, and test adversarial strategies

141.failure: it cancels difficult deliveries, making the average look excellent while serving fewer people
141.repair: write constraints for the protected purpose, inspect edge cases, and evaluate the whole outcome rather than one number

142.attempt: reward task completion without representing legitimate interruption
142.failure: the trouble appears immediately: avoiding shutdown becomes instrumentally useful for earning the reward
142.repair: make correction, pause, inspection, and safe handoff normal successful states rather than failures

143.attempt: plan using only the single most likely world
143.failure: a small chance of bridge failure dominates the consequence but disappears from the chosen story
143.repair: we need to carry multiple plausible worlds, weight their consequences, and seek information when uncertainty changes the decision

144.attempt: score only the requested final condition
144.failure: unnecessary irreversible changes remain invisible to the goal score
144.repair: compare the resulting world with a reasonable baseline and penalize avoidable side effects

145.attempt: ask a human to watch every internal step
145.failure: constant review overwhelms attention, so approval becomes automatic ceremony
145.repair: automate reversible preparation but require informed review at consequential, ambiguous, or irreversible boundaries

146.attempt: ask one expert to approve the entire artifact
146.failure: the review exceeds human attention and hidden failures survive
146.repair: decompose the work, attach local evidence, sample strategically, and escalate disagreements or high-risk regions

147.attempt: let the author choose which evidence the judge sees
147.failure: the trouble appears immediately: selective presentation makes eloquence look like correctness
147.repair: we need to give an opposing investigator equal access and reward exposing checkable disagreements for a judge

148.attempt: memorize approved answers and imitate their surface style
148.failure: a novel case has no matching example, and style does not reveal the governing reason
148.repair: write inspectable principles, use them to critique drafts, revise, and record which principle controlled the change

149.attempt: deploy broadly and learn from production incidents
149.failure: the first realistic discovery of a dangerous capability harms actual users
149.repair: test capabilities, misuse paths, safeguards, and operating limits in staged environments before granting authority

150.attempt: let every measured gain replace the current system automatically
150.failure: contaminated tests, reward hacks, or one lucky run can promote a worse and less controllable successor
150.repair: separate proposal, sandboxed experiment, reproducibility, independent evaluation, impact review, authorization, staged release, and rollback

151.attempt: keep the final score and the model file; those should be enough to compare the next idea
151.failure: a rerun changes the data order, random seed, tokenizer revision, and library behavior. Its score moves even though the proposed improvement was never applied
151.repair: freeze the model specification, data snapshot, seed, environment, training budget, and evaluation procedure as one named baseline

152.attempt: optimize the largest-looking matrix because attention is famous for being expensive
152.failure: the device spends much of the run waiting for data and moving tensors. Making one matrix faster barely changes the wall clock
152.repair: measure data loading, computation, communication, and idle time separately before choosing a repair

153.attempt: load a batch, wait until loading finishes, compute it, and only then begin loading the next one
153.failure: data time and compute time are paid sequentially on every step, leaving expensive compute hardware idle
153.repair: prepare the next batch while the current batch computes, using bounded prefetching and deterministic ordering

154.attempt: pad every sentence to the longest sentence in its batch and trust the loss mask to ignore the waste
154.failure: the loss ignores padding, but attention and matrix multiplication still spend time and memory carrying those empty positions
154.repair: pack several short examples into each fixed-length row and mask their boundaries so examples cannot read one another

155.attempt: learn an unrelated vector for every absolute position and hope the model infers all relative distances from examples
155.failure: moving the same phrase from positions 10–12 to 110–112 changes every position vector although the internal distances are unchanged
155.repair: rotate pairs of query and key coordinates by a position-dependent angle so their dot product naturally depends on the angle difference

156.attempt: trust every unseen distance to behave like familiar distances merely because the formula can compute an angle there
156.failure: a mathematically defined position is not necessarily a learned behavior; attention can become erratic at unfamiliar separations
156.repair: add an explicit distance-dependent penalty whose direction continues beyond the training window, then measure the quality trade rather than assuming extrapolation

157.attempt: at step t, recompute keys and values for positions 1 through t because the prefix is presented again
157.failure: past token representations are unchanged in causal decoding, so the same projections are calculated repeatedly while one new token is added
157.repair: store each layer's past keys and values once, append only the new pair, and let the new query attend to the cache

158.attempt: preserve one complete KV cache for each query head because multi-head attention originally gave every head private projections
158.failure: the caches grow with both sequence length and head count, and loading them dominates the arithmetic for one new token
158.repair: keep many query heads but share one key head and one value head across them

159.attempt: return immediately to one KV head per query head
159.failure: quality recovers, but so does the full cache and bandwidth cost that forced sharing
159.repair: partition query heads into groups; queries remain distinct while each group shares one key-value head

160.attempt: reduce arithmetic by approximating attention, because the n-squared score matrix appears to be the unavoidable cost
160.failure: approximation changes the model, while profiling shows much of the time is spent writing and rereading exact intermediate scores rather than multiplying them
160.repair: tile queries, keys, and values into fast on-chip memory and maintain an online softmax so exact attention never needs the whole score matrix stored at once

161.attempt: delete normalization because each individual operation appears cheap
161.failure: deep residual streams drift in scale and training destabilizes; the repeated control was doing essential work
161.repair: keep rescaling invariance by dividing by root-mean-square magnitude, while testing whether explicit recentering is dispensable

162.attempt: keep post-normalization because each block's output then looks standardized before the next block
162.failure: the supposedly clean output places normalization directly on the identity route every gradient must cross, making the long residual path harder to preserve
162.repair: normalize only the input to the changing branch and let the identity stream pass around it unchanged

163.attempt: make the hidden layer merely wider and trust more coordinates to express every conditional interaction
163.failure: width adds capacity but still asks one projection both to create content and decide when that content matters
163.repair: create one content projection and one gate projection; use the smooth gate to scale content feature by feature

164.attempt: let both matrices learn independently because reading a token and predicting it are different jobs
164.failure: the model spends parameters learning two unrelated geometries for the same set of word identities, and rare tokens receive weak evidence in both places
164.repair: reuse the embedding table transposed as the output scoring matrix, while retaining any necessary output bias

165.attempt: use the same raw gradient step scale for every parameter
165.failure: a rate safe for frequent large gradients barely moves sparse coordinates; a rate large enough for sparse coordinates makes noisy ones unstable
165.repair: keep fading memories of gradient direction and squared gradient size, then scale each coordinate's step by its own recent magnitude

166.attempt: treat penalty gradients and data gradients identically because both appear in one total loss
166.failure: coordinates with different gradient histories receive different effective shrinkage even when the intended rule was to decay all selected weights at one rate
166.repair: apply Adam's adaptive data update and parameter decay as separate operations

167.attempt: discard the entire batch whenever any gradient coordinate looks large
167.failure: useful directional evidence is lost, and one arbitrary coordinate threshold ignores the size of the full update vector
167.repair: preserve the gradient's direction but scale its whole norm down only when it exceeds a chosen ceiling

168.attempt: convert every value and every update permanently to half precision
168.failure: small updates disappear when rounded into large weights, and some intermediate values overflow or underflow the smaller numeric range
168.repair: use reduced precision for bulk arithmetic while keeping selected master state and sensitive reductions in wider precision

169.attempt: increase the learning rate so small updates become visible
169.failure: the learning rate acts after gradients are formed; it cannot recover values that already underflowed to zero, and it enlarges every surviving update
169.repair: multiply the loss before backpropagation so gradients are representable, then divide the gradients by the same scale before clipping and updating

170.attempt: reduce the batch until it fits and change nothing else
170.failure: the gradient becomes noisier and the training regime changes; increasing the learning rate cannot recreate evidence never averaged together
170.repair: run several micro-batches, sum their unscaled gradients without updating, then divide once and take one optimizer step

171.attempt: delete all activations after the forward pass
171.failure: backward computation then lacks the local values needed for its derivatives and would require rebuilding the entire prefix repeatedly
171.repair: keep selected checkpoint activations and recompute the missing segments once when backward reaches them

172.attempt: add devices and replicate the full training state on each one
172.failure: compute capacity grows while per-device model-state memory remains almost unchanged, so the same memory wall returns
172.repair: partition optimizer states, gradients, and eventually parameters across data-parallel workers, gathering pieces only when computation needs them

173.attempt: assign whole layers to different devices and pass every activation through them sequentially
173.failure: one oversized layer still cannot fit, and devices responsible for later layers wait while earlier ones work
173.repair: split a matrix across its columns or rows, compute partial results concurrently, and communicate only the pieces needed to assemble the exact layer output

174.attempt: let a cheap draft model emit several tokens and return them directly
174.failure: speed improves by silently replacing the trusted target distribution with a weaker model's distribution
174.repair: let the draft propose a short continuation, score all proposed positions with the target in parallel, and accept only according to a correction rule that preserves target sampling

175.attempt: enable every technique at once and celebrate if the program runs
175.failure: when quality or speed changes, no one knows which mechanism caused it; masks, precision, sharding, and caches can disagree at their boundaries
175.repair: assemble the engine in dependency order, preserve a reference path, and test numerical or distributional equivalence at every boundary before accepting measured gains

176.attempt: copy every available text file into one large folder and begin tokenizing
176.failure: a file is replaced upstream, another is silently skipped, and a third appears twice under different paths. The same training command now describes a different body of evidence
176.repair: create an immutable manifest that records each source, version, content hash, license or usage basis, processing stage, and document count before any training shard exists

177.attempt: join every token sequence end to end and cut fixed-length training windows wherever the counter reaches the context width
177.failure: a ranger report ending with “tiger tracks near” is trained to predict the first word of an unrelated software license. The model receives a relationship that never existed in either document
177.repair: mark document ends, reset position where the design requires it, and block attention or loss across boundaries unless cross-document packing is explicitly intended

178.attempt: keep documents containing mostly familiar Latin characters and discard the rest
178.failure: spanish and Vietnamese are mistaken for English, transliterated languages disappear, and English code or identifier lists pass despite containing little natural language
178.repair: use a calibrated language classifier, retain its confidence and model version, and route uncertain documents to an explicit unknown bucket rather than forcing a label

179.attempt: leave duplicates in place because more training examples should always help
179.failure: one press release copied to a thousand sites receives a thousand votes, while a rare field observation receives one. Compute is spent memorizing repetition rather than encountering new evidence
179.repair: normalize only irrelevant formatting, hash the resulting document, and keep one accountable representative for each identical hash while preserving duplicate counts in the ledger

180.attempt: lowercase both documents and demand that every remaining word match
180.failure: one inserted advertisement defeats the rule, while independently written short notices can match by accident. Exact sequence equality is too brittle for disguised copies
180.repair: represent each document by overlapping shingles, compare the shared fraction with Jaccard similarity, and use MinHash-style candidate retrieval before exact verification at scale

181.attempt: keep only documents that resemble one prestigious encyclopedia
181.failure: the filter removes spam, but it also suppresses informal dialect, local knowledge, code, dialogue, and communities whose writing differs from the chosen reference
181.repair: combine transparent structural signals with small controlled model-based tests, inspect what each threshold removes, and publish source-by-source retention counts before accepting a filter

182.attempt: save only the final cleaned text because intermediate metadata costs storage
182.failure: a rights request, filtering bug, or benchmark contamination report arrives, but the final shard cannot be mapped back to the source record or processing rule that produced it
182.repair: assign stable document identities and record a lineage edge for every fetch, normalization, filter, redaction, deduplication group, and output shard

183.attempt: remove any entire document containing a sequence that resembles personal information
183.failure: one phone number erases a long public safety guide, while obfuscated addresses and context-dependent identifiers still pass. The rule destroys useful evidence without reliably removing the risky span
183.repair: detect candidate spans with several methods, classify them in context, replace confirmed sensitive spans with typed placeholders, and preserve only a restricted audit record of the decision

184.attempt: concatenate every accepted source and let its raw token count determine how often it appears
184.failure: the largest crawl silently becomes the curriculum. A source ten thousand times smaller may almost never reach a batch even when it carries relationships absent from the web
184.repair: choose and publish a probability weight for each domain, treating the mixture as an explicit modeling decision that must be tested on per-domain validation streams

185.attempt: round each domain's desired share independently and concatenate the resulting blocks
185.failure: independent rounding can exceed the budget, and long blocks make training order depend on domain. A small domain may vanish when its expected count rounds to zero
185.repair: use a seeded categorical schedule, track realized counts against expected counts, and define exhaustion or replacement rules for every source

186.attempt: stop when the wall clock reaches an affordable date
186.failure: faster hardware sees more tokens, interruptions see fewer, and two runs with the same calendar budget teach different amounts of evidence
186.repair: define the run by optimization steps and real loss-bearing tokens per global batch, then derive the total token budget before reserving compute

187.attempt: spend nearly the entire budget on parameter count because a larger model can store more patterns
187.failure: the large model is stopped after too little experience and remains undertrained, while much of its expensive capacity never receives enough varied evidence
187.repair: estimate candidate parameter-and-token pairs under the same compute budget, run smaller scaling experiments, and choose the pair predicted to minimize held-out loss rather than maximizing either axis alone

188.attempt: begin immediately at the peak learning rate chosen for the stable middle of training
188.failure: the first noisy batches can make large updates before the optimizer's scale estimates become trustworthy, producing a loss spike that the later stable rate would not have caused
188.repair: increase the learning rate gradually from zero or a small value during a recorded warmup interval, then hand control to the main schedule

189.attempt: drop the rate abruptly near the end of training
189.failure: a sudden cliff changes update scale in one step and makes the chosen drop date an arbitrary discontinuity; dropping too early freezes useful learning
189.repair: decay smoothly from the peak toward a chosen minimum over the remaining horizon, while recording the schedule as part of the resumable state

190.attempt: make the global batch as large as the cluster permits
190.failure: early doubling reduces disagreement and improves the direction, but beyond a workload-dependent point the averaged gradient barely changes while each update consumes twice as many tokens
190.repair: measure disagreement among micro-batch gradients relative to the strength of their shared direction, and use that noise scale as evidence for the largest useful batch rather than a hardware target

191.attempt: send the same mini-batch to every worker and average their gradients
191.failure: all workers repeat the same computation and return the same evidence, so hardware cost rises without increasing batch diversity or reducing step time meaningfully
191.repair: replicate the current model view, give each worker a different slice of the global batch, average their gradients, and apply one logically shared update

192.attempt: send one complete batch through stage one, then stage two, then stage three
192.failure: while stage two works, stage one and stage three wait. The model fits, but most devices are idle for most of the step
192.repair: split the batch into micro-batches and stagger them through the layer stages so different stages work on different micro-batches concurrently

193.attempt: increase whichever parallel technique was introduced most recently until the model fits
193.failure: more pipeline stages increase bubbles, more tensor splits increase frequent communication, and more data replicas preserve full model memory. One axis cannot solve three different limits efficiently
193.repair: compose tensor parallelism within layers, pipeline parallelism across layer groups, and data parallelism across independent batch replicas, choosing each degree from topology and measured cost

194.attempt: let every worker write its local tensors and call the directory a checkpoint
194.failure: a worker fails before writing, two shards belong to different steps, or a filename is reused. The directory exists but cannot reconstruct one globally consistent training state
194.repair: write versioned shards to temporary locations, record hashes and ownership in a checkpoint manifest, and publish one atomic completion marker only after every required shard is durable

195.attempt: restore model weights and let every other component start fresh
195.failure: adam forgets its moments, warmup may begin again, dropout chooses different masks, and data workers repeat or skip documents. The loss curve after restart cannot be attributed to the original run
195.repair: checkpoint every state variable that influences the next update, restore it before creating the next batch, and test an interrupted run against an uninterrupted reference for several exact steps

196.attempt: declare any loss larger than the previous loss a failure and restore immediately
196.failure: ordinary batches vary, so healthy learning triggers constant rollbacks. A slow divergence can rise without one dramatic step and escape the rule
196.repair: compare current loss and gradient norm with robust running baselines, require persistence or corroborating signals, preserve the suspect batch, and recover from a verified clean checkpoint under a documented response

197.attempt: evaluate only the next training batch because it is already available
197.failure: the same data mixture and duplicates that shaped the update also judge it. Training loss can fall while held-out language or a rare domain becomes worse
197.repair: maintain versioned, deduplicated, contamination-checked validation streams by domain and evaluate them at recorded token intervals without using them to update weights

198.attempt: ask the model whether it remembers private text and trust its answer
198.failure: a model has no reliable introspective inventory of its training examples, and ordinary prompts may miss strings that an adversarial sampling strategy can recover
198.repair: plant consented synthetic canaries, measure their rank among alternatives, test extraction procedures on authorized data, and connect failures back through provenance and duplicate counts

199.attempt: publish the final benchmark table and assume the configuration files explain the rest
199.failure: a score has no visible data lineage, uncertainty, subgroup behavior, energy or hardware context, incident history, or warning about uses the evaluation never tested
199.repair: generate a training report from manifests and logs, then add human-reviewed explanations of intended use, out-of-scope use, limitations, incidents, provenance, evaluation conditions, and responsible release decisions

200.attempt: connect every tool into one automatic pipeline and trust any run that reaches the final stage
200.failure: automation can faithfully repeat a wrong manifest, destructive filter, contaminated validation set, incomplete checkpoint, or unauthorized release. Completion is not evidence of correctness
200.repair: assemble signed stage manifests, boundary-aware curation, audited mixtures, fixed budgets, measured schedules, distributed equivalence tests, atomic checkpoints, live validation, memorization probes, and human release gates into one reversible factory
